→ D1 (concedes): Conceded as to the request and its timing: the rider did name Paya Lebar Square at 12:21 and the driver accepted at 12:21 on a complete, timestamped record (F9, F10, F11). Naming a place exempts the route to that place and the stop, not every kilometre driven afterwards — the reach of that consent is the issue, and it is limited by its own words '3-4 minutes' (F9). [F9 F10 F11] [RD-3 RD-5]
→ D2: The premise is right but the conclusion overreaches: RD-3(a) exempts the segment serving the named point, and the track shows that segment added 2.97 km while covering 4.57 km of road against an optimal 1.60 km, straying up to 729 m off the corridor (F4); a named-stop consent cannot cover driving that far away from both the optimal route and the named point. claims.assertion: The trip was driven 19.0 km against an optimal 15.5 km, i.e. 3.5 km (+22%) of excess distance, and took 33.2 min against a 21.8 min estimate (F1, F3).

The GPS track contains one off-route segment, 12:25–12:36, in which 4.57 km was driven where the optimal route covers only 1.60 km, adding 2.97 km and straying up to 729 m from the optimal route (F4). Under RD-1 this is an un-exempted off-route segment unless an exemption applies.

The rider did name a stop — 'Can you stop at Paya Lebar Square? I need to grab a parcel, 3-4 minutes.' — and the driver agreed 'Ok can' at 12:21, both before the segment began at 12:25 (F9, F10, F4). This is a specific-places authorisation (RD-3(a)); it exempts only the route to that named point plus the 4-minute stop, not any further deviation.

The stop itself lasted 4 min 0 s at 12:28–12:32 at a point 5890 m from pickup and 4243 m from drop-off (F2), matching the '3-4 minutes' the rider asked for, so the stop duration is within the rider's own request and attracts no in-trip waiting charge on a service where only the $5 pickup waiting fee is published.

The driver's only justification for the route is 'The rider asked me to stop at Paya Lebar Square, so I drove there and waited' (F12); a claimed permission to stop does not cover the 729 m lateral deviation and 2.97 km extra on the segment (F4), and no verbal-agreement defence is available to him (G11).

No traffic exemption applies: there were no traffic incidents recorded near the route in the trip window (F15), the only speed records are bands 5 (40–49 km/h, PIE) and 4 (30–39 km/h, CTE) (F13, F14), which are not bands 1–2 and in any case are not tied to the replaced portion of the optimal route (RD-4(b) does not exempt on its own), and weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain (F16).

Because this is a metered RydeTAXI trip, the un-exempted segment's extra kilometres entered the fare: the fare billed 18.95 km of distance for $26.72 and separately billed $4.91 of excess distance at $1.4100/km (F8, F5), matching 3.48 km of excess.

The refund on the un-exempted segment is the segment's extra_km × this trip's per-km rate = 2.97 km × $1.4100/km = $4.19 (F4, F5, F8); the residual excess shown in the fare ($4.91 minus $4.19) is attributable to the sanctioned stop and map-matching jitter within the route corridor and is not claimed.

The waiting fee of $1.15 billed as 4.4 min × $0.26/min (F6) covers the in-trip stop of 4 min 0 s (F2); on a metered RydeTAXI the meter's waiting unit is chargeable under RD-3(c), so no refund is sought for it.

The rider has 3.8 years on the platform, a 5.0 rating and no disputes or upheld findings in 90 days (F17), while the driver has one dispute in 90 days and no upheld route finding (F18); on this record this is a first upheld deviation for the driver, so a flag_account action under RD-6 is not requested.

weaknesses: The rider did ask for the Paya Lebar Square stop and the driver agreed (F9, F10), so the other side will argue the whole 12:25–12:36 segment is the rider's own requested detour and exempt under RD-3(a); our answer relies on reading the request as naming a place and duration ('3-4 minutes') only, which is a reading of the message text (F9) rather than a system record.

The stop was 5890 m from pickup and 4243 m from drop-off (F2) and the segment ran 12:25–12:36 with the vehicle stationary only 12:28–12:32 (F2, F4), so part of the 4.57 km could be ordinary driving toward the destination rather than a loop; the judge may find the portion attributable to the deviation smaller than 2.97 km, reducing the award below $4.19.

Many of the off-route segment's 2.97 extra km may be shared with the agreed stop route and with the general flow of traffic (F13, F14 show 30–49 km/h bands on the expressways), which the driver will use to argue the deviation was neither gratuitous nor costly; RD-2 itself declines to refund corridor jitter, so the computable refund is small relative to the rider's expectation of a 'much more' fare.

The rider's complaint says the fare was 'much more than the estimate' (F1: 19.0 vs 15.5 km; F3: 33.2 vs 21.8 min), but a fixed-fare service would owe nothing for distance — here the recoverable meter excess is only $4.19 (F4, F5), so the client's expectation of a large refund is not supported by the policy.

I need to grab a parcel, 3-4 minutes", and the driver accepted at 12:21 (F10); the chat record is complete and every message is timestamped (F11).

The rider named the location, so under RD-3(a) the segment serving that rider-named stop does not constitute a deviation from the shortest route, and her consent was given before the segment began: the consent message is timestamped 12:21 (F9) while the off-route segment only runs 12:25–12:36 (F4).

The single off-route segment lasts 11 minutes (12:25–12:36) and contains a 4-minute stationary period at 12:28–12:32 away from any pickup or drop-off point (F2), i.e. the stop the rider herself requested; the driver's written statement matches this and is corroborated by the GPS record, not contradicted by it (F12).

The 11.4 minutes the trip ran over the estimate (F3) are explained by the 4 minutes of stationary stop (F2) and by the congestion on the actual route corridor — Pan Island Expressway band 5, 40–49 km/h, and Central Expressway band 4, 30–39 km/h, both during 11:58–12:48 (F13, F14) — so no unexcused driving time is attributable to the driver.

No traffic incident was recorded near the route in the trip window and the weather was fair with no rain (F15, F16), so the driver does not claim a blocked-road exemption; the deviation is justified by the rider's own stop request, not by traffic.

This is a metered RydeTAXI trip, so the wait during the rider-requested stop is lawfully billed at the meter's waiting unit: $1.15 for 4.4 minutes at $0.26/min (F6), matching the 4 min 0 s stationary period at the stop (F2).

Billing carried no surge (multiplier 1.0×) and the total of $40.74 is fully itemised as base $3.90 + distance $26.72 for 18.95 km + time $7.50 + waiting $1.15 + platform $1.47 (F7, F8), so there is no unpublished or unexplained add-on for FARE-1 to strike out.

At most the billed excess distance over the optimal route is $4.91 (3.48 km × $1.41/km, F5) against an actual excess of 3.5 km over 15.5 km (F1), and that residual is consumed by the rider-named Paya Lebar Square stop (F2, F4, F9); the driver's account has no upheld dispute in the last 90 days (F18), so no account flag under RD-6 is warranted.

Neither the chat messages nor the rider's complaint contains any threat, intimidation, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation — the complaint only disputes the fare (F9, F10) — so no SAFE-1 or SAFE-2 escalation is required.

points.response: Conceded as to the request and its timing: the rider did name Paya Lebar Square at 12:21 and the driver accepted at 12:21 on a complete, timestamped record (F9, F10, F11). The premise is right but the conclusion overreaches: RD-3(a) exempts the segment serving the named point, and the track shows that segment added 2.97 km while covering 4.57 km of road against an optimal 1.60 km, straying up to 729 m off the corridor (F4); a named-stop consent cannot cover driving that far away from both the optimal route and the named point. The rider's authorisation is tied by its own text to a '3-4 minute' stop (F9), corroborated by the 4 min 0 s stationary period (F2), so kilometres beyond reaching and leaving that point remain unexempted under RD-3(b) and RD-5.

The stop is not in dispute: 4 min 0 s stationary at 12:28–12:32, 5890 m from pickup and 4243 m from drop-off (F2), matching the rider's own '3-4 minutes' (F9) — which is exactly why the unused 12:25–12:28 and 12:32–12:36 portions of the segment still have to be explained under RD-1. The driver's statement (F12) asserts only that he drove to Paya Lebar Square and waited; it says nothing about the 729 m lateral excursion in F4, and his 'the rider asked' account cannot supply consent to a route change the rider never authorised (RD-5).

The congestion cited is not severe by the policy's own measure: bands 5 (40–49 km/h) and 4 (30–39 km/h) (F13, F14) sit above the band 1–2 levels RD-4(b) contemplates, and RD-4(b) never exempts on its own; with no incident recorded (F15) and fair weather (F16), traffic gives no excuse for any kilometre. Duration is also not what is claimed: even subtracting the 4 min stop from the 11.4 min overshoot (F3, F2) leaves roughly 7 minutes of extra driving time unaccounted for.

Agreed and it cuts against the driver: with no incident (F15) and fair weather (F16), the only exemption candidate is the rider's stop request, which as shown reaches only the detour to and from the named point and the four minutes there (F9, F2, F4).

Not contested: on a metered RydeTAXI the in-trip stop's waiting unit is chargeable and $1.15 for 4.4 min at $0.26/min (F6) matches the 4 min stop (F2); the rider seeks no refund of the waiting fee, only of the unexempted extra kilometres under RD-2.

Accepted that the bill is itemised with no surge (F7, F8), but that is beside the point: this is a metered trip, so the excess distance line of $4.91 for 3.48 km at $1.4100/km (F5) is precisely the extra-charge RD-2 makes refundable when the kilometres behind it are unexempted.

The driver's own number is the concession: he accepts the billed excess distance over the optimal route is $4.91 for 3.48 km (F5) against +3.5 km actual (F1), and the 4-minute stop (F2) cannot consume 2.97 km of driving that took the car up to 729 m off the corridor (F4) — at $1.41/km that segment's extra distance alone is 2.97 × 1.4100 = $4.19 under RD-2. I withdraw nothing but narrow one point in the client's favour of a clean number: the determinable unexempted extra distance is the segment's 2.97 km at this trip's rate of $1.4100/km (F4, F5), giving $4.19, and I do not chase the residual between that and the billed $4.91 (F5) because RD-2 excludes corridor jitter and the portion attributable to reaching the named point.

The excess distance (F1) and excess duration (F3) are not disputed as measurements, but RD-1 asks whether each off-route segment is explained, and the single segment (F4) coincides with the stop the rider herself named and timed at 12:21 (F9), so the numbers alone do not establish an unexcused breach.

C2 is conceded as far as the segment's measurements go — one segment, 12:25–12:36, 2.97 km added, up to 729 m off the optimal route (F4) — but the existence of the segment triggers RD-3/RD-5 review, and RD-1 leaves no room for the rider's implicit claim that the metres of the segment can be severed from the stop that created it.

We agree the rider named the place and the driver accepted before the segment began (F9, F10, F4), but RD-3(a)'s exemption is triggered by the rider naming the place — which she did — and RD-2's own text declines to refund the residual gap between the billed excess and the sum of the segments, which is where the rider's remaining $0.72 sits.

The 4 min 0 s stationary period (F2) fits the rider's own '3-4 minutes' (F9), and on a metered RydeTAXI the meter's waiting unit is chargeable under RD-3(c); the $1.15 waiting fee (F6) is lawfully billed, as the rider's own C9 concedes.

The driver does not rest on any verbal agreement — he relies on the rider's own written message naming the place (F9), which is a record, not a statement; his written statement (F12) adds nothing the GPS does not already show.

We do not claim a traffic exemption: no incident was recorded (F15), the speed bands were 4 and 5, not 1–2 (F13, F14), and the weather was fair (F16), so RD-4 does not apply — the driver's justification is the rider's own stop request under RD-3, not traffic.

The billed figures are accurate — 18.95 km distance for $26.72 and $4.91 of excess distance at $1.4100/km (F8, F5) — but RD-2 refunds only kilometres on an un-exempted segment, and the segment at F4 is the rider-named stop.

This is the rider's weakest step: it takes 2.97 km as un-exempted while simultaneously conceding (C3, C7) that the rider named the stop and that part of the excess is hers to bear, and RD-2 caps any refund at the sum of un-exempted segments' extra_km — the rider has identified no un-exempted kilometre, so the computable refund is zero.
